android.widget.TextView.text: Nicholas Boys Smith

android.widget.TextView.text: Japan’s Himeji Castle is said to resemble a bird in flight - Alamy
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Which of the world’s man-made creations merit jet fumes, bumpy roads and holidaying hordes to ogle and touch? My list is below. Yours may differ, but I would proffer two ideas.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Firstly, there is wisdom in crowds. Clichés are clichés for a reason. If everyone says it is wondrous and beautiful, statistically, you will probably agree. What humans find moving and marvellous is remarkably predictable. Don’t fear mass appeal.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Secondly, if in doubt go sacred. Many of the world’s most transporting buildings are religious, self-consciously juxtaposing great scale with coherent detail and ornament to evoke the eternal. Buildings that successfully dignify the human condition move us in ways that buildings that honestly express their construction never can.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Great Pyramid of Giza, Egypt, c.2560 BC
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Visitors travel by camels in the area where the pyramids are located, including the largest pyramid of Cheops, also known as The Great Pyramid of Giza
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: The Great Pyramid of Giza is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World - Anadolu via Getty Images/Murat Gok
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: The photos cannot do it. You know them too well. You have to visit to be awestruck by the sheer scale of the thing. Herodotus related that 100,000 labourers took 20 years to pull and pile the stone, for him a textbook example of cruel non-Greek ways. Standing minuscule beside the oldest and only surviving of the Seven Wonders of the World, you can understand.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: The Pantheon, Rome, c.AD 118-126
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Interiors of Pantheon in Rome, Italy
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Inside Rome’s magnificent Pantheon - iStockphoto/Vladislav Zolotov
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: There is nowhere greater to stand than directly under the oculus at the centre of
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Rome’s
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: peerless Pantheon. The dome is the largest unreinforced concrete dome that has or will ever be created. It is a mingled miracle of heavenly symbolism and earthly engineering. Coffers, hidden internal chambers and porous pumice stone lighten the central load where the dome is most vulnerable to collapse.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: The best way to preserve a building is to sanctify and use it, not pickle it in unchanging “heritage”. The Pantheon survives because the former temple became a church in AD 609 and has been continually repaired ever since. Astonishingly, the original bronze Roman doors still serve. Outside, immense granite Egyptian columns stand sentry, seemingly for eternity.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Hagia Sophia, Istanbul, AD 532-537
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Hagia Sophia, Istanbul
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Hagia Sophia is a monument of Byzantine architecture and art - skaman306/Teerayut Chaisarn
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: No building stands as firmly at the crossroads of history, geography, religion and civilisation as Hagia Sophia. The Byzantine Empire’s former
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: , site of a church for over a millennium, yanked violently into a new life as the Ottomans’ great mosque after the 1453 sack of Constantinople, a museum for 85 years after the secularising Kemal Atatürk, the Hagia Sophia has been redesignated as a mosque since 2020. Like the nearby Bosphorus, history eddies past.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: I will never forget entering for the first time: the huge and spreading pendentive dome (the world’s first at this scale), the sudden dark after the sunshine outside, receding as my eyes adjusted and the golden mosaics, colours, basket capitals, saints and angels emerged from the stygian gloom.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Ely Cathedral, Britain, from AD 1083
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: The Octagon Tower of Ely Cathedral, Cambridgeshire, England, UK
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Ely Cathedral’s Octagon Tower - Alamy/Martin Bache
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Rising above the frigid East Anglian fens, Ely’s greatest glory grew from catastrophe. In 1322 its Norman crossing tower collapsed. It was replaced with an oak octagon, lead-covered from above, luminous from below, which is unparalleled in any church in any nation. Unusually we know the names of the architect and carpenter who conceived and shaped this miracle: Alan of Walsingham and William Hurley.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Piazza San Marco, Venice, 11th to 16th centuries
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Piazza San Marco is the historic heart of Venice
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Piazza San Marco is the historic heart of Venice - Moment RF
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Not St Mark’s sinuous Basilica, nor the
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Doge’s Palace
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: , heavy with Republican power, not the towering Campanile, nor the delicate Logetta, not the elaborate Clocktower, nor the Piazzetta with its heart-stopping lagoon views, not Sansovino’s proud Zecca
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: nor the enveloping Ala Napoleonica which finalises the enclosure, but all of it, every brick and stone and column of it, make Piazza San Marco, the world’s greatest town square.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: It defies words. It defines urban beauty. Even Napoleon, no romantic, who gaily murdered the Venetian Republic, was moved to wonder by the place. Its buildings drip with riches. My favourite is the porphyry statue of the four tetrarchs. You can sit beside and touch their toes.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Angkor Wat, Cambodia, early 12th century
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Angkor Wat
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world - Moment RF/Tumjang
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: No single edifice challenged European assumptions of their own cultural superiority as effortlessly as this 12th-century, initially Hindu, now Buddhist, temple city (the name’s meaning) emerging from the Cambodian forests.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Imagine the stupefaction of an early 16th-century Portuguese visitor: “It is not possible to describe it with a pen... it is like no other building in the world.” A Victorian added: “It is grander than anything left to us by Greece or Rome.” Angkor Wat is the world’s largest religious complex and, uniquely in this list, features on its nation’s flag.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Sainte-Chapelle, Paris, 1240s
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: The interior of the Saint Chapelle, Paris, France
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Sainte-Chapelle’s ceilings feature deep blue ribbed arches decorated with golden stars - RooM RF/RilindH
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: The world’s jewel box is
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: France’s
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: former royal chapel, commissioned by Louis IX to rhyme with royal chapels in Venice, Aachen and Constantinople.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Emerging via a tight spiral staircase from the ill-lit lower chapel into Sainte Chapelle is a passage from night to day, from earth to heaven, from sin to salvation. Polychromatic light scatters through the vast rayonnant windows with their web of bar-tracery. The bright blue ceiling twinkles with a thousand painted stars. Don’t forget to breathe.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Revolutionary thugs vandalised the chapel in the 18th century, but fortunately 19th-century French Gothicists, including a young Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, restored it with love and colour.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Clermont-Ferrand Cathedral, France, begun in 1248
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Clermont-Ferrand Cathedral. Clermont-Ferrand, Auvergne-Rhone-Alpes, France
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Clermont-Ferrand Cathedral is built entirely in black Volvic lava stone - benkrut
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Most Gothic cathedrals climb into the clouds with pinnacles of pale stone. Clermont does it in black. Begun in 1248, Notre-Dame-de-l’Assomption is built from the dark volcanic lava of nearby Volvic, its twin spires rising over an equally volcanic landscape.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: The second surprise is inside. Against almost black piers, medieval stained glass ignites in reds, blues, greens and golds: colours made brighter by the surrounding darkness.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: The Duomo, Florence, 1296-1436
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Beautiful sunset cityscape view of the Santa maria nouvelle Duomo and the town of Florence, in the Italian Tuscany.
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Brunelleschi’s Dome is an iconic Renaissance structure - Suttipong Sutiratanachai
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: It does not matter whether buildings are too big. It matters if they are too ugly. Florence Cathedral took 140 years to build. You can see why. It dominates the still physically
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Renaissance city
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: leering over its medieval streets or suddenly blocking the vista as you turn a corner. Nobody minds. The delicate marble panels in alternating white, green or pink are too beautiful for complaint.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Above it all rises Brunelleschi’s Dome, reaching for the heavens and announcing that mankind had achieved again the lost knowledge of the ancients.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Forbidden City, Beijing, from 1406
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Imperial Palace and the Forbidden City
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Beijing’s Forbidden City is an imperial palace complex of the Ming and Qing dynasties - Moment RF/Jackyenjoyphotography
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Strictly, this is not one building but 980, with 8,886 rooms.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Beijing’s
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Forbidden City is a labyrinth within a city within a city: a vast, symmetrical sequence of courts, gates and halls laid out along an imperial axis, the scale reducing as you progress from the expansive to the intimate.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Its other genius is colour. Vermilion walls and columns, the colour of fire, blaze beneath yellow-glazed roofs, the emperor’s colour, while blue, green and gold crowd the painted brackets beneath. Built for the Ming emperors, this is hierarchy, procession and etiquette frozen into bricks and tiles.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Chateau de Chenonceau, Loire Valley, mid 16th century
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Exterior view of Chateau de Chenonceau
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Chateau de Chenonceau was built on the foundations of an old watermill - Alamy/JHVEPhoto
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: The Chateau de Chambord is bigger and more illustrious, but no French chateau catches the breath as effortlessly as Chenonceau.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: A rich cream cake of flamboyant Gothic forms and Renaissance classical solecisms, Chenonceau is not just a building but a bridge over the river Cher, whose rippling and reflecting waters double the number of oriel and oeil-de-boeuf windows visible from the riverbanks. It is ludicrously romantic.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: The chateau, an escape route between Nazi-occupied and Vichy France in war, was unkindly treated by the 20th century. Flooded and bombed, it is now miraculously renatured, a renaissance chateau in date and deed.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Himeji Castle, Japan, 1601-1609
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Himeji Castle with beautiful cherry blossom
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Himeji Castle surrounded by cherry blossom - Alamy/Jui-Chi Chan
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Military buildings should not look so good. Himeji is a great white apparition of layered roofs and plastered walls, earning its nickname White Heron Castle.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Beauty conceals purpose. Gates, narrow passages and bewildering turns were designed to confuse attackers as they climbed towards the keep. Yet the whole defensive machine seems almost weightless, like a bird about to take flight.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Taj Mahal, India, 1632-1653
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Taj Mahal in morning light. Located in Agra, India
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: The Taj Mahal was made a Unesco World Heritage Site in 1983 - adamkaz
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Description seems superfluous so iconic is the world’s greatest witness to love, Shah Jahan’s tomb for his late wife, Mumtaz Mahal.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Everyone recognises this marble marvel with its sinuous central dome and its four surrounding smaller domes or
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: . But the genius of the thing is in the detail from up close not just the form from afar. Inlays, tessellations, interlocking patterns, plant motifs, four-pointed stars and elaborate lattice windows abound. They are somehow both overwhelming and restrained. First visiting as a cynical 19-year-old, I was dumbstruck.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Castle Howard, Yorkshire, begun 1699
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Castle Howard from the air with the Atlas Fountain
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Castle Howard appeared as Evelyn Waugh’s Brideshead on screen - CAG Photography Ltd/Charlotte Graham
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: No building could be less typical of the dour Yorkshire temperament than the 3rd Earl of Carlisle’s flamboyant, almost megalomaniac, palace. Sir John Vanbrugh and Nicholas Hawksmoor’s first collaboration and masterpiece is too princely to be convincingly English.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: It has a screen
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: as Evelyn Waugh’s tragic Brideshead, in the 1981 TV series. Devastated by fire in 1940, had the modern National Trust owned it, it would have been left a ruin. Instead, it is slowly being rediscovered.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Neuschwanstein Castle, Bavaria, from 1869
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Neuschwanstein, Bavaria
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Neuschwanstein is the world’s tallest castle - Alamy /Alpineguide
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Neuschwanstein
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: is the Platonic idea of a romantic castle. Straddling two steep cliffs in the Alpine foothills, the world’s tallest castle is crammed, inside and out, with turrets, pinnacles, lancets, gables and sculptures. It is all a gleeful fake, a medieval castle built in the 19th-century age of iron with borrowed money by Ludwig II, one of the last Bavarian kings.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: La Sagrada Família, Barcelona, from 1882
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: La Sagrada Familia
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: La Sagrada Família, Gaudí‘s magnum opus - Sylvain Sonnet
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Begun in 1882 as a conventional Gothic church in a Latin cross shape,
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: La Sagrada Família
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: was transformed by Antoni Gaudí into one of the world’s most ambitious and recognisable buildings. It combines Gothic aspiration, Christian symbolism, Catalan craft and forms drawn from nature. Columns branch like trees. Stone seems to grow.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: The building’s high nave rises as a forest of tapering trunks reaching towards the canopy of light. There are 52 columns within, one for each Sunday of the year, holding up the high roof, and no flying buttresses despite its soaring height.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Outside, six stupendous towers now dominate
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Barcelona’s
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: skyline, held up by the church’s 16 central columns. This is an engineering high-wire act of space-age ambition, all evolved by a model-building recluse in a workshop without computers or calculators.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Woolworth Building, New York, 1910-1913
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Aerial view of the Woolworth Building in downtown Manhattan, New York City
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: New York’s Woolworth Building was nicknamed the ‘Cathedral of Commerce’ - Alamy/Felix Lipov
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: American know-how created skyscrapers: the safety elevator in New York and the steel frame in
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: . Early skyscrapers were Gothic. Pointing heavenwards, echoing medieval cathedrals, their vertical thrust was judged perfect for their scale and function.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Cass Gilbert’s mesmerising Woolworth Building emulated Charles Barry’s Victoria Tower in Westminster but is over twice the height. Limestone and terracotta-clad and immensely decorated with piers, pinnacles and ogee arches, the Woolworth Building briefly defined New York.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: In an alternative, steam-punk world in which modernism never happened, skyscrapers would have been beautiful. Many might have emulated Gilbert’s Manhattan masterpiece.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Milan Central Railway Station, Italy, 1906-1931
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Interior view of the monumental Milan Central Railway Station in Italy
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Milan Central Railway Station features marble halls with decorative mosaics - iStockphoto/wsfurlan
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Thank heavens the Victorians invented railways. Once upon a time, it was normal, indeed necessary, to create new infrastructure which was beautiful and functional.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: The world’s most awe-inspiring railway terminus is probably the cavernous and effortlessly baroque Milano Centrale called
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: (Life in Motion) by its primary architect, Ulisse Stacchini. Walking through the stupendous portico and into the endless halls you feel suddenly at the wrong scale, like Alice in Wonderland.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Lutyens’ Delhi, India, 1912-1931
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Rashtrapati Bhavan is the official home of the President of India
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Rashtrapati Bhavan, the former Viceroy’s House during the British Raj - saiko3p
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Last and greatest of the British Empire’s physical creations, New Delhi’s government precinct is the world’s most successful instance of one man single-handedly creating a new architectural style.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Edwin Lutyens, very possibly England’s greatest ever architect, presided with others, notably Herbert Baker, helping with secondary buildings. Greatest of all is the Rashtrapati Bhavan, which, for 16 brief years, was the Viceroy’s House before the sun set on British rule.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Frauenkirche, Dresden, reconstructed 1994-2005
android.widget.TextView.heading: true

android.widget.Image.content-desc: Frauenkirche (Church of Our Lady) - Dresden, Germany
android.widget.Image.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Frauenkirche was reconstructed after RAF bombing in 1945 - Jorg Greuel
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Dresden’s overwhelmingly beautiful Frauenkirche astonishes. Be-domed and baroque, it appears Catholic and 18th century. In fact, it is Lutheran and the church you see today is modern, the greatest building completed in our lifetimes.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Shattered by RAF bombing in 1945, a popular and locally led campaign
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: funded and reconstructed the church
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: . Architects and elite left-wing opinion objected. But the people insisted. At the reconsecration, the packed congregation inside was joined by an estimated 60,000 townsfolk outside. Many wept. About two million visit each year. Join them.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.view.View.text: Nicholas Boys Smith is the founder and chairman of Create Streets and visiting professor of architecture at the University of Strathclyde.

android.widget.TextView.text: The World's Largest Beaver Dam Is Tucked Away In Canada's Largest National Park
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Rene Bennett
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Dennis MacDonald/Shutterstock
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Cathedrals, castles, and skyscrapers are architectural wonders we visit in modern cities, but nature has its own architects that have raised impressive structures in the Canadian wilderness. In northern Alberta, a colony of industrious beavers has constructed a dam that's visible from outer space. From end to end, the beaver dam is about 2,543 feet (almost a half mile) long, according to
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Parks Canada
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: , making it the world's largest. If you laid the Empire State Building on its side without its spire and antenna, the dam would be over twice as long. The mammoth structure is in the
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.view.View.content-desc: wildlife-filled Wood Buffalo National Park, which also happens to be Canada's largest national park
android.view.View.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: wildlife-filled Wood Buffalo National Park, which also happens to be Canada's largest national park
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: . Given that sheer space, the dam is not an easy sight to reach — it sits in the middle of the park, away from road or trail access. You're most likely to see it only by plane or helicopter.
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: In beaver real estate, building dams allows the animals to turn shallow streams into ponds and expand their territory. They live in the resulting ponds, serving as cover from predators and a place to store food. A dam as massive as the one at Wood Buffalo wasn't built by a single family of beavers, but rather is the result of multiple generations of beavers. Ecologist Jean Thie — who discovered the dam in 2007 while scouring satellite images — told
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: The Independent
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: that the dam has likely been under construction since the mid-1970s. It sits at the base of the Birch Mountains, where runoff comes down from higher ground and spreads across the flat terrain, per
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: Canadian Geographic
android.widget.TextView.heading: false

android.widget.TextView.text: . That helps explain why the dam got so big: The beavers had to keep extending their dam sideways to keep water from trickling around its ends.

android.widget.TextView.text: The world's largest beaver dam sits in the southern part of Wood Buffalo National Park, in a remote stretch of boreal forest, wetlands, and muskeg. Parks Canada gives visitors two options for reaching it: Trek for days through waterlogged terrain, or charter a private sightseeing plane. For most travelers, the flight is the only feasible choice. There's no dam parking lot, nor even a dam trailhead. A private bush plane or flight tour can take you over this isolated corner of the park, so you can see the dam's long profile aerially against the surrounding bog and forest.
